Headline: Why unfinished tasks nag at you
Fact: In 1927, psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik described how interrupted or unfinished tasks are easier to remember than completed ones. The idea began when her professor, Kurt Lewin, noticed a waiter who remembered unpaid orders in detail but forgot them as soon as the bill was settled.
Source title: Zeigarnik Effect – Psychology Today

Headline: The IKEA effect
Fact: People tend to value things more when they’ve built them themselves. In studies where participants assembled IKEA boxes, folded origami and built Lego, they valued their own (often wobbly) creations more highly – even rating them close to experts’ work. Researchers named it the IKEA effect.
Source title: The IKEA effect: When labor leads to love (Norton, Mochon & Ariely, 2012) – Harvard DASH

Headline: Now you’ll see it everywhere
Fact: Ever learn a new word and then spot it everywhere? That’s the frequency illusion, also called the Baader-Meinhof phenomenon – your attention has simply been tuned to notice it. The nickname appeared in 1994, and Stanford linguist Arnold Zwicky later coined the term ‘frequency illusion’.
Source title: What is the Baader-Meinhof Phenomenon? – Macquarie University Lighthouse

Headline: The magic number seven (or four?)
Fact: In 1956, psychologist George Miller famously suggested we can hold about seven items, plus or minus two, in short-term memory. Later research by Nelson Cowan and others suggests the real limit for young adults is closer to about four ‘chunks’ of information.
Source title: George Miller’s magical number of immediate memory in retrospect (Cowan, 2015) – PubMed Central

Headline: Familiar feels friendly
Fact: Simply seeing something again and again tends to make us like it more – even things we barely notice. Psychologist Robert Zajonc named this the mere-exposure effect in 1968, and it’s one reason catchy songs and familiar logos grow on us.
Source title: Mere-exposure effect – Wikipedia

Headline: Say the colour, not the word
Fact: Try naming the ink colour of the word RED printed in green – it’s surprisingly hard! John Ridley Stroop published this in 1935: reading is so automatic that the word gets in the way of naming the colour. Psychologists still use the test today.
Source title: The Stroop effect’s long (and colorful) influence – American Psychological Association

Headline: About 150 friends
Fact: Anthropologist Robin Dunbar compared primate brain sizes with the size of their social groups and predicted that humans can keep up about 150 stable relationships. It’s known as Dunbar’s number – though not every researcher agrees the limit is fixed.
Source title: Are humans limited to 150 friends? – Live Science

Headline: The forgetting curve
Fact: In 1885, Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory and found that we forget new information quickly at first, and then the loss levels off – the ‘forgetting curve’. He also found that spreading study out over time helps you remember far more.
Source title: 4.7: Ebbinghaus – LibreTexts Cognitive Psychology

Headline: Faces everywhere
Fact: Ever spotted a face in a power point or a slice of toast? That’s face pareidolia. Researchers at UNSW Sydney found our brains process these ‘fake’ faces using the same visual mechanisms we use for real ones.
Source title: Why the brain is programmed to see faces in everyday objects – UNSW Sydney

Headline: Why did I come in here?
Fact: Walked into a room and forgotten why? Psychologist Gabriel Radvansky found that walking through a doorway can make us forget, because the mind treats the doorway as an ‘event boundary’ and files away what happened in the last room.
Source title: Why walking through a doorway makes you forget – Scientific American

Headline: Hearing your name across the room
Fact: In a noisy room you can tune in to one voice and ignore the rest. Colin Cherry named this the ‘cocktail party problem’ in 1953. In a 1959 follow-up, about a third of people even noticed their own name in a conversation they were ignoring.
Source title: Cocktail party effect – Wikipedia

Headline: Honest placebos still help
Fact: Placebos can help even when people know they’re placebos! In a 2010 Harvard study, people with irritable bowel syndrome took pills clearly labelled ‘placebo’ – and nearly twice as many reported real relief as people who got no treatment.
Source title: Placebos work – even without deception – Harvard Gazette

Headline: The smoke-filled room
Fact: In a 1968 study, students filled in forms while smoke poured into the room. People on their own usually reported it, but in groups of three, someone spoke up in only three of the eight groups – even once the room was full of smoke. It’s called the bystander effect.
Source title: How the social context influences helping – Principles of Social Psychology

Headline: The tower that keeps growing
Fact: When the Eiffel Tower opened in 1889 it stood 312 metres tall. Thanks to radio and TV antennas added in 1957, 2000 and 2022, it now reaches 330 metres – and its iron even gains a few millimetres in the summer heat before shrinking again in winter.
Source title: Why does the Eiffel Tower change size? – Official Eiffel Tower website

Headline: The Opera House is cut from one sphere
Fact: Jørn Utzon spent years trying to work out how to build the Sydney Opera House’s sail-like shells. His breakthrough was the ‘spherical solution’: every shell is shaped from the surface of the same sphere, which finally made the curved roof possible to build.
Source title: The spherical solution – Sydney Opera House

Headline: The glue that failed upwards
Fact: In the late 1960s, 3M chemist Spencer Silver was trying to make a super-strong adhesive and accidentally made a weak one that could stick and unstick again and again. Years later, his colleague Art Fry used it to make bookmarks that wouldn’t slip out at church – and the Post-it Note was born.
Source title: Art Fry & Spencer Silver – Lemelson-MIT

Headline: The Golden Gate’s happy accident
Fact: The Golden Gate Bridge’s famous ‘International Orange’ started out as a primer. When the steel arrived coated in reddish-orange protective paint, consulting architect Irving Morrow decided he liked it – it stood out in the fog and suited the hills, sea and sky.
Source title: Golden Gate Bridge surprising facts – HISTORY

Headline: A church 140+ years in the making
Fact: Construction of Barcelona’s Sagrada Família began on 19 March 1882, and Antoni Gaudí took over the project the following year. He devoted the rest of his life to it, and building has carried on for a full century since his death in 1926.
Source title: History of the Basílica – Sagrada Família

Headline: The Tube map is a circuit diagram
Fact: Harry Beck, an electrical draughtsman for the London Underground, redesigned the Tube map based on the circuit diagrams he drew for his day job – ignoring real distances in favour of neat, coloured lines. First printed in 1933, his design still shapes the map today.
Source title: Harry Beck’s Tube map – Transport for London

Headline: 410 days to the sky
Fact: The 102-storey Empire State Building in New York went up in just 410 days. Builders used an assembly-line approach, and when it opened in 1931 it was the tallest skyscraper in the world.
Source title: 10 surprising facts about the Empire State Building – HISTORY

Headline: Helvetica’s secret first name
Fact: Helvetica began life in 1957 as Neue Haas Grotesk, designed by Max Miedinger with Eduard Hoffmann at the Haas type foundry in Switzerland. It was later renamed Helvetica, from Helvetia – the Latin name for Switzerland.
Source title: Helvetica – Wikipedia

Headline: Tallest for 3,800 years
Fact: The Great Pyramid of Giza originally stood about 146.6 metres tall and was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years – until the spire of England’s Lincoln Cathedral overtook it around 1300.
Source title: Great Pyramid of Giza – Wikipedia

Headline: Leaning from the start
Fact: The Leaning Tower of Pisa began tilting while it was still being built. By 1178, only a few storeys up, it was already sinking unevenly into the soft clay, sand and shells beneath it. Wars then paused the work, and the tower took about two centuries to finish.
Source title: Why does the Leaning Tower of Pisa lean? – HISTORY

Headline: Why QWERTY?
Fact: The QWERTY layout comes from Christopher Latham Sholes’s typewriters of the 1870s. After around 30 test models it settled into the arrangement we still type on 150 years later – though historians still argue about exactly why the letters ended up where they are.
Source title: Where did the QWERTY keyboard come from? – Smithsonian Magazine

Headline: A house on a waterfall
Fact: The Kaufmann family asked Frank Lloyd Wright for a weekend house near their favourite waterfall in Pennsylvania – so in 1935 he designed one right on top of it. At Fallingwater, the stream flows underneath the house, and you can hear it inside.
Source title: Fallingwater – Britannica

Headline: The first emoji
Fact: The first popular emoji set was 176 tiny pictures, each drawn on a 12 × 12 pixel grid by Shigetaka Kurita for the Japanese phone company NTT DOCOMO in 1999. In 2016, New York’s Museum of Modern Art added all 176 to its collection.
Source title: Shigetaka Kurita. Emoji. 1998–1999 – MoMA

Headline: Wombats make cube-shaped poo
Fact: Bare-nosed wombats are the only animals known to produce neat, cube-shaped poo. Researchers found the cubes take shape inside the wombat’s roughly 10-metre-long intestines – not at the exit, as people once guessed – as the poo dries out and the gut walls contract.
Source title: Scientists get to the bottom of wombat cubed poo mystery – University of Tasmania

Headline: The throw that changed the javelin
Fact: In 1984, East Germany’s Uwe Hohn threw the javelin 104.80 metres – so far that throws risked flying beyond the safe space inside stadiums. In 1986 the men’s javelin was redesigned, with its centre of gravity moved 4 cm forward, so his mark will likely never be beaten.
Source title: Javelin Throw – World Athletics

Headline: A day on Venus outlasts its year
Fact: Venus spins so slowly that one full rotation takes about 243 Earth days – but it travels around the Sun in just 225. That means a day on Venus is longer than its year! It also spins backwards, so the Sun rises in the west.
Source title: All About Venus – NASA Space Place

Headline: The record that won’t budge
Fact: The men’s javelin world record of 98.48 metres was set by Czech legend Jan Železný in Jena, Germany, on 25 May 1996. It has stood ever since – no one has thrown the modern javelin further.
Source title: Men’s javelin throw world record – World Athletics

Headline: Three hearts and blue blood
Fact: Octopuses have three hearts: two pump blood through the gills and a third sends it around the body. Their blood is blue, too, because it carries oxygen using a copper-based protein called hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin.
Source title: Eight strange and wonderful facts about octopuses – Shedd Aquarium

Headline: The javelin champ who tried baseball
Fact: Soon after winning Olympic gold in Atlanta in 1996, javelin world-record holder Jan Železný had a tryout as a pitcher with baseball’s Atlanta Braves. He had barely played the sport, but the coaches were surprised by how quickly he picked it up.
Source title: In 1996, the Braves tried to turn the world’s best javelin thrower into a pitcher – MLB.com

Headline: Honey that never goes off
Fact: Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs that were thousands of years old and still preserved. Honey keeps so well because it holds very little water, is naturally acidic, and contains hydrogen peroxide made with the help of an enzyme from bees.
Source title: The science behind honey’s eternal shelf life – Smithsonian Magazine

Headline: Ancient javelins had a secret strap
Fact: In the ancient Olympic pentathlon, athletes threw the javelin using a leather strap called an ankyle. Wrapped around the shaft near its centre of gravity, with two fingers hooked into its loop, it helped the javelin fly further and steadier.
Source title: The Ancient Olympics: Pentathlon – OpenLearn (The Open University)

Headline: Sharks are older than trees
Fact: Sharks’ ancestors were swimming the seas around 450 million years ago, while the first trees appeared roughly 385–390 million years ago. The catch: today’s ‘modern’ sharks only arose about 195 million years ago, so it depends what you call a shark!
Source title: Are sharks really older than trees? – Live Science

Headline: Bananas are berries
Fact: Botanically speaking, bananas are berries but strawberries aren’t! A true berry grows from a single flower with one ovary and has fleshy layers around its seeds. Strawberries grow from a flower with many ovaries, so they’re a different kind of fruit.
Source title: Why are bananas berries but strawberries aren’t? – Live Science

Headline: Hotter than the Sun
Fact: A lightning bolt can heat the air around it to about 28,000 °C (50,000 °F) – much hotter than the surface of the Sun. That sudden heat makes the air expand explosively, which is the boom we hear as thunder.
Source title: Severe Weather 101: Lightning – NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory

Headline: First throw, world record
Fact: The women’s javelin world record is 72.28 metres, thrown by Barbora Špotáková of the Czech Republic in Stuttgart on 13 September 2008. She did it with her very first throw of the competition – in damp conditions that usually aren’t good for javelin.
Source title: Women’s javelin throw report, 13 Sep 2008 – World Athletics

Headline: India’s golden throw
Fact: At the Tokyo 2020 Olympics, Neeraj Chopra won the men’s javelin with a throw of 87.58 metres. It was India’s first-ever Olympic gold medal in athletics.
Source title: Javelin champion Chopra wins India’s first Olympic gold in athletics – World Athletics

Headline: The bishop used to be an elephant
Fact: Before it was a bishop, this chess piece was an elephant! In shatranj, the Persian ancestor of chess, it was called pīl, which became al-fil (‘the elephant’) in Arabic. Spanish players still call the bishop alfil, and Russian players call it slon, meaning elephant.
Source title: Shatranj – Wikipedia

Headline: Cleopatra and the Moon landing
Fact: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the 1969 Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. The pyramid was finished around 2560 BC – roughly 2,500 years before her time – while Apollo 11 landed about 2,000 years after it.
Source title: Did Cleopatra really live closer in time to the first lunar landing than the Great Pyramids? – WorldAtlas

Headline: Monopoly’s forgotten inventor
Fact: Monopoly grew out of The Landlord’s Game, invented by Lizzie Magie to show how land monopolies made a few people rich at everyone else’s expense. She was granted a US patent for it on 5 January 1904 – before American women even had the national right to vote.
Source title: Lizzie Magie – Wikipedia

Headline: Oxford is older than the Aztecs
Fact: Teaching was already happening at the University of Oxford by 1096. The Aztec capital, Tenochtitlán, wasn’t founded until about 1325 – more than two centuries later – which makes Oxford older than the Aztec Empire.
Source title: What university is older than the Aztec Empire? – Britannica

Headline: Tetris came from a Soviet lab
Fact: Tetris was created in 1984 by Alexey Pajitnov, a programmer at the computing centre of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Today the game is part of the collection at New York’s Museum of Modern Art.
Source title: Alexey Pajitnov. Tetris. 1984 – MoMA

Headline: The shortest war in history
Fact: The Anglo-Zanzibar War, fought on 27 August 1896 between Britain and the Sultanate of Zanzibar, is widely considered the shortest war ever recorded. It was over in less than 45 minutes.
Source title: Anglo-Zanzibar War – Britannica

Headline: When a computer beat the champion
Fact: In 1997, IBM’s Deep Blue beat world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game rematch – the first time a reigning world champion lost a match to a computer under tournament conditions. A year earlier, Kasparov had won their first match 4–2.
Source title: Deep Blue – IBM History

Headline: Napoleon wasn’t actually short
Fact: Napoleon’s height was recorded as 5 feet 2 inches – but in old French units, which were longer than British ones. Converted, he was about 1.67 metres, a little above average for a Frenchman of his time. British cartoonist James Gillray helped make the ‘tiny Napoleon’ myth stick.
Source title: Napoleon complex: was he short? – HISTORY

Headline: God’s number is 20
Fact: A Rubik’s Cube has more than 43 quintillion possible positions, yet in 2010 a team of researchers proved every single one can be solved in 20 moves or fewer. Puzzlers call this ‘God’s number’.
Source title: God’s Number is 20 – cube20.org

Headline: Mammoths met the pyramids
Fact: Woolly mammoths were still alive after the Great Pyramid was built! A small population survived on Wrangel Island, off Siberia, until about 4,000 years ago – centuries after the pyramids of Giza went up.
Source title: Woolly mammoth extinction – National Geographic

Headline: The game nobody wanted
Fact: Scrabble was invented by Alfred Mosher Butts, an architect left out of work by the Great Depression. He first called it Lexiko, then Criss-Cross Words, and game companies kept turning it down. It only became Scrabble after he teamed up with James Brunot.
Source title: Alfred Butts – Lemelson-MIT

Headline: A game about karma
Fact: Snakes and Ladders began in India as Moksha Patam, a game about good and bad deeds: ladders lifted you up for virtues, and snakes dragged you down for vices. It was brought to the United Kingdom in the 1890s.
Source title: Snakes and ladders – Wikipedia

Headline: Who are the kings?
Fact: In traditional French playing cards, each king was named after a legendary ruler: the king of hearts was Charles (Charlemagne), spades was the biblical King David, diamonds was Julius Caesar and clubs was Alexander the Great.
Source title: Who do the kings, queens and jacks represent? – International Playing-Card Society

Headline: The newest card in the deck
Fact: The joker joined the deck in the mid-1800s, when American players of the card game euchre wanted an extra top trump called the ‘best bower’. Card maker Samuel Hart printed the first illustrated one, his ‘Imperial Bower’, in 1863.
Source title: Joker (playing card) – Wikipedia

Headline: Landing on their feet
Fact: Cats can twist in mid-air to land on their feet, thanks to the ‘righting reflex’. Kittens start to show it at just 3–4 weeks old and have it mastered by 6–9 weeks, helped by an unusually flexible spine.
Source title: Cat righting reflex – Wikipedia
